attempts.label: CRCNS:fcx-1
attempts.paper_title: Network Homeostasis and State Dynamics of Neocortical Sleep
attempts.entry_title: Network homeostasis and state dynamics of neocortical sleep (Watson et al. 2016)
attempts.summary: The paper's central finding, that sleep evens out cortical firing as fast-firing pyramidal cells slow down and slow-firing cells speed up, held up in this data across sleep and within nonREM packets (first-to-last packet slope 0.872), as did the overall decline in population rate. The reported drop in rate variability over sleep and the firing changes within single UP states did not reproduce. Most of the lasting effects of individual sub-states (REM, microarousals, waking between packets) did not reproduce, likely because the paper does not say how sequences of states were formed and no rule gave its cell counts. Lower firing in waking after sleep held only weakly, as most cycles lack scored waking right after sleep.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Watson, Levenstein, Greene, Gelinas and Buzsaki (2016) on CRCNS data set fcx-1, which holds the spike trains, scored brain states, detected UP/DOWN states and spindles, and LFP of 27 frontal cortex recordings in 11 rats. It compares firing rates across states, their changes over sleep and within nonREM episodes and packets, the LFP and UP/DOWN dynamics, and the rate changes across sleep sub-state triplets.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Watson et al. (2016) from CRCNS fcx-1

outcomes.statement: The data comprise 11 rats, 27 sessions and 54 WAKE-SLEEP episodes, with 995 putative pyramidal cells (mean 36.9 per session, range 10 to 104) and 126 putative interneurons (4.67 per session, range 0 to 13).
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states, and Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Table S1
outcomes.quote: This resulted in 995 putative pyramidal (pE) cells (mean of 36.9 cells/session ... 10-104) and 126 putative interneurons (pI) (4.67 cells/session ... 0-13)
outcomes.notes: 995 pE and 126 pI cells (mean 36.85 pE per session, range 10 to 104; pI mean 4.67, range 0 to 13), 27 sessions and 11 rats match exactly. The WAKE-SLEEP cycles in _WSRestrictedIntervals.mat number 51, not 54; each session's Wake and Sleep intervals are exactly its WakeSleep pairs (51, 51 and 51 in all), with no unpaired WAKE or SLEEP, so no cycle was lost in parsing. The criterion names no partial outcome; partial is given because five of six counts match, and whether a partial rule applies is asked of a reader.

outcomes.statement: There are 790 microarousals, with median duration 15.9 s, 0.32 per minute, taking 9.1% of SLEEP time; the fraction of time in MA decreases over nonREM episodes but not over SLEEP.
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of brain states; Table S1
outcomes.quote: There were a total of 790 MAs in our dataset (median duration = 15.9±3.3sec; frequency = 0.32±0.12 per minute; 9.1±3.5% of time in SLEEP). Over nonREM episodes the fraction of time occupied by MAs decreased (correlation versus normalized nonREM episode time

statistics.about: MA time fraction against normalized nonREM episode time

outcomes.notes: 434 MA intervals lie inside SLEEP (2130 in the files). Median duration 11.0 s over all MAs (11.5 s over session medians), per-session median incidence 0.184 per minute, per-session median 3.70% of SLEEP, against 790, 15.9 s, 0.32 and 9.1%; none within tolerance. The MA fraction falls over normalized episodes (20 bins, bin means R = -0.956, p = 4.5e-11; 10 bins R = -0.970, p = 3.3e-06), and over SLEEP the bin means are not significant (p = 0.15, 0.098; pooled period-bins p = 0.0057, 0.00061). The criterion names no partial outcome; partial is given because the trends hold and the four values do not. The 345 WakeInterruptions shorter than 40 s are not MAs by the paper's definition, since none lies between two packets (123 between two REM intervals, 80 between REM and a packet). Variant, MA reading (b), counting them as MAs, 779 events, 0.318 per minute (within tolerance), median 13.0 s, 7.85% of SLEEP, episodes R = -0.960 (p = 1.9e-11), SLEEP p = 0.93. With the Dino ACC sessions left out, episodes R = -0.949 (p = 1.7e-10), SLEEP p = 0.089.
deviations: The episode correlation uses the MA fraction in 10 or 20 normalized bins, both as bin means over episodes and as pooled episode-bins, as the criterion allows; episodes include MA and packet seconds.

outcomes.statement: nonREM packet durations span two orders of magnitude with a median of 111 s.
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of brain states; Table S1
outcomes.quote: We found that the duration of packets was distributed over two orders of magnitude, with a median of 111 seconds
outcomes.notes: Median of the 701 packets in SLEEP 111.0 s. Longest over shortest 52.5 (14 to 735 s), less than the two orders of magnitude of the statement, which the criterion only reports.

outcomes.statement: Per-cell mean firing rates of pyramidal cells are strongly positively skewed and span three orders of magnitude, from 0.05 to 5 Hz, with medians of 0.76 Hz in WAKE, 0.69 Hz in nonREM and 0.88 Hz in REM; interneuron medians are 5.59, 4.69 and 4.25 Hz.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure 2A; Figure S2C
outcomes.quote: the distribution of per-cell mean firing rates for putative pyramidal neurons was strongly positively skewed ... spanning three orders of magnitude range from 0.05 Hz to 5 Hz ( Figure 2A ). Median rates (±SD) of putative pyramidal cells in each state were: WAKE: 0.76±1.53 Hz, nonREM: 0.69±0.86 Hz, REM: 0.88±1.33 Hz; and for putative interneurons were: WAKE: 5.59±7.25 Hz, nonREM: 4.69±5.62 Hz, REM 4.25±9.43 Hz
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) medians pE 0.755, 0.706, 0.936 Hz and pI 6.001, 4.565, 5.724 Hz; reading (b) pE 0.784, 0.691, 0.922 and pI 5.632, 4.637, 5.724. Five of six within 10% under both; pI REM is 5.724 against 4.25. pE skew 2.18 to 2.83. The 1st to 99th percentile range covers 0.05 to 5 Hz within 10% in WAKE (0.004 to 7.14 Hz, reading b) and REM (0.008 to 6.03) but not nonREM (0.014 to 4.17; 4.05 under reading a); 5th to 95th percentiles stop below 4.5 Hz in every state. The criterion requires the shape for both the reproduced and the partial outcome, so the outcome is not reproduced. Whether the range applies to each state, when the paper itself says the nonREM tail is shorter, is asked of a reader. The pI REM median is equal under both readings because the middle cell is the same (Dino_061814_mPFC cell 46, 5.706 and 5.743 Hz in its two cycles); reading (a) has no duplicated rows.
deviations: The range test is applied in each state, as the criterion's 'in each state' reads.

outcomes.statement: Per-cell nonREM and WAKE rates are highly correlated (R = 0.82), but the slope of their relation is below 1 (95% interval 0.66 to 0.71), so state transitions affect cells differently across the rate spectrum, fast cells decreasing and slow cells increasing in nonREM.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure 2B and legend
outcomes.quote: Whereas nonREM and WAKE firing rates remained highly correlated on a per-cell basis (R = 0.82, p < 1 −10 ), the slope of this relationship significantly deviated from 1 ( Figure 2B ), demonstrating that state transitions exert a differential effect across the firing rate spectrum (95% confidence interval of slope ... 0.66 - 0.71)

statistics.about: correlation of nonREM and WAKE rates
slope of nonREM rate on WAKE rate

outcomes.notes: Reading (a) slope of log10 nonREM on log10 WAKE 0.684 (0.661 to 0.708), R 0.803; reading (b) 0.687 (0.658 to 0.717), R 0.824. Linear rates give slope 0.45. 82% of cells above the median WAKE rate fire less in nonREM, 55% of those below fire more.

outcomes.statement: The right tail of the rate distribution is longer in WAKE and REM than in nonREM; the fraction of pE cells above 2 Hz is 19.2% in WAKE and in REM and 8.8% in nonREM.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: The right tail extended toward higher rates during WAKE and REM compared to nonREM ( Figure 2A ; fraction of >2 Hz neurons
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) 18.8% WAKE, 20.6% REM, 9.3% nonREM; chi-square nonREM against WAKE p = 4.1e-16, against REM p = 4.4e-21. Reading (b) fractions 18.4, 19.5, 9.1% with p = 3.2e-09 and 8.3e-11.

outcomes.statement: The burst index (fraction of spikes with ISIs below 15 ms) is highest in nonREM (median 11.8%), lowest in WAKE (4.0%), with REM (5.5%) slightly above WAKE.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states
outcomes.quote: Burst index was highest during nonREM (median in nonREM = 11.8%) and lowest during WAKE (4.0 %), with REM (5.5 %) slightly higher than WAKE (p < 0.05; Kruskal-Wallis test)
outcomes.notes: Medians (nonREM, WAKE, REM) reading (a) 6.26, 2.43, 3.56%; (b) 4.93, 1.58, 2.33%; (c) 11.47, 4.51, 6.39%. Kruskal-Wallis p from 3.4e-46 to 3.6e-54; REM above WAKE by Dunn (p 1.3e-06 to 1e-05) and rank-sum. The order and the tests hold under every reading; no reading puts all three medians within tolerance.
deviations: Reading (c), the fraction of spikes with an ISI <= 15 ms before or after them, is added from the Results' wording, 'the fraction of spikes with ISIs below 15 ms' (Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states), beside the claims file's readings of a proportion of ISIs.

outcomes.statement: Average pE autocorrelograms peak at about 8 ms in nonREM and show smaller peaks near 125 ms (theta) in REM and WAKE, and decay faster in nonREM (median fit exponent -1.35) than in WAKE (-0.83) and REM (-0.80).
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: a large peak occurred at approximately 8ms inter-spike interval during nonREM, whereas smaller peaks were present at ~125 ms (i.e., theta frequency) during REM and WAKE ( Figure 2C ). ... Time decay of the autocorrelograms of pyramidal neurons was significantly faster during nonREM compared to WAKE and REM ( Figure 2C ; decay fit exponent median nonREM = - 1.35, WAKE = - 0.83, REM = - 0.80; p < 0.05; Kruskal-Wallis test)
outcomes.notes: Average nonREM autocorrelogram peaks at 8.5 ms; WAKE and REM have local maxima at 125 and 126 ms (nonREM also at 125 ms). Median decay, reading (a) WAKE -0.108, nonREM -0.538, REM -0.169; (b) -0.118, -0.336, -0.112; (c) -0.582, -1.623, -0.574. nonREM is the most negative and Kruskal-Wallis p <= 1.7e-95 under all three; no medians within tolerance. Cells with fewer than 100 counts dropped (158 of 995 in WAKE, 131 in nonREM, 284 in REM). The 125 ms bump is small, the average autocorrelogram at 115 to 135 ms being 1.027 (WAKE), 1.026 (REM) and 0.981 (nonREM) times its mean at 80 to 100 and 150 to 170 ms; the local-maximum test also fires at 125 ms in nonREM.
deviations: Per-cell peaks are found on a 5 ms boxcar-smoothed autocorrelogram in 1 to 50 ms, and cells with fewer than 100 counts are dropped; both are standard choices the paper does not state.

outcomes.statement: Population synchrony (fraction of pE cells firing in 50 ms windows) has a skewed distribution; more than 15% of pE cells rarely fire synchronously with others (in 4% of windows) while fewer than 4.2% fire synchronously in at least half of the windows.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure S2F
outcomes.quote: The fraction of principal cells firing in 50 ms overlapping time windows ('population synchrony') showed a skewed distribution. More than 15% of principal neurons rarely fired synchronously with others (4% of windows), while less than 4.2% discharged synchronously in at least half of the windows
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) 62.9% of pE cells fire with another pE cell in at most 4% of windows and 0.00% in at least half; reading (b) 54.2% and 0.00%. Per-cell distributions skewed (2.31, 2.26); population synchrony per window skew 1.28. The criterion's bounds hold with wide margins.

outcomes.statement: DOWN state durations are skewed with a median of 0.19 s and UP state durations with a median of 0.47 s.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure S4A; Table S1
outcomes.quote: The durations of DOWN states of 'slow oscillations' showed a skewed distribution (median = 0.19s) and so did the UP states (median = 0.47s; Figure S4A )
outcomes.notes: Deposited detections, 43230 UP and 86839 DOWN states (the paper's counts exactly), medians 0.473 and 0.188 s, skew 2.56 and 2.15. All start inside scored packets of the cycles.
deviations: Uses the deposited UP/DOWN detections (_UPDOWNINtervals.mat), reading (a) of updown-durations; a new detection was not run, since the LFP reduction kept has no power above 100 Hz.

outcomes.statement: Within UP states, firing rates of pyramidal cells and interneurons decrease over the course of the UP state, with decreasing E/(E+I) ratio and decreasing pE population synchrony; UP states begin with a surge of gamma power followed by increased sigma power.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure 1E
outcomes.quote: UP states were characterized by an initial surge of gamma power, followed by increased sigma power ( Figure 1E ), corresponding to UP state-related sleep spindles. Firing rates of both pyramidal cells and interneurons decreased over the time course of the UP state, accompanied by a decreasing gain of excitation (excitatory-inhibitory, E-I, ratio) and decreasing population synchrony of pyramidal neurons
outcomes.notes: Per normalized bin over 43230 UP states, pE rate 1.823, 1.359 ... 1.310, 1.619 Hz (last not below the first two; R = -0.293); pI 15.88 to 11.63 Hz (R = -0.983); synchrony 0.079 to 0.071 (last below first two, R = -0.447); E/(E+I) 0.373 to 0.396 (R = +0.470). Sigma power peaks in bin 0 and gamma in bin 3, the reverse of the statement. Two of four measures decrease and the spectral order fails.
deviations: The criterion's 50 ms bins for synchrony and E/(E+I) are taken as the 10 normalized UP-state bins (47 ms for a median UP state).

Gamma and sigma power come from an 8 ms band-power series (4th order Butterworth, mean of the squared signal) on goodeegchannel, log10 and z-scored per session; the paper's spectrogram method is not given.
Uses the deposited UP/DOWN detections (_UPDOWNINtervals.mat), reading (a) of updown-durations; a new detection was not run, since the LFP reduction kept has no power above 100 Hz.

The 8 ms series is zero-phase band-passed, which at 9 to 25 Hz spreads power over tens of ms, so the sigma peak in the first bin may carry power from the DOWN-UP edge; the outcome fails on the pE rate and E/(E+I) regardless.

outcomes.statement: In the early UP state pE cells fire in sequences stable across the first and second halves of SLEEP, and a cell's onset latency is negatively correlated with its firing rate.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure 2D and 2E
outcomes.quote: pyramidal neurons fired in reliable spatiotemporal sequences during the early part of the UP state (<200 msec) and these stereotypical sequences remained stable across the entirety of sleep ( Figure 2D ). Additionally, the spike onset times of individual neurons in the sequences were negatively correlated with their firing rates
outcomes.notes: First and second half latencies correlate across cells, R = 0.733 (halves of each SLEEP, n 932) and 0.660 (halves of the session, n 758). Latency against log10 WAKE rate R = -0.127, p = 7.6e-05; against log10 nonREM rate R = -0.238, p = 6e-14. Per session the WAKE-rate correlation is negative in 20 of 27 sessions.
deviations: A cell's mean latency in a half is computed when it has at least 5 UP states with a spike within 200 ms (a standard choice).

outcomes.statement: In nonREM, pairwise spike-count correlations depend on firing rate group; pairs within the fastest group and within the slowest group are positively correlated, fast-firing pairs most highly, and fast and slow cells are negatively correlated with each other.
outcomes.source: Results, Assessment of firing patterns in different brain states; Figure 2F
outcomes.quote: the fastest and slowest firing neurons tended to be positively correlated within groups, but were actually negatively correlated across groups ( Figure 2F )
outcomes.notes: Mean 100 ms count correlations in nonREM, WAKE sextiles, 6-6 0.0328 (p = 2.9e-70), 1-1 0.0062 (p = 2.1e-20), 1-6 0.0064 (p = 2e-12, positive). Correlations rise with rate group across the whole matrix; no negative group pair. nonREM sextiles, the claims file's reading (b) for this figure, give 1-6 0.0095 (p = 8.5e-66).
deviations: Sextiles follow M2. Reading (a) ranks each pE cell's rate over all scored WAKE of its session (before round 1's revision, the mean of its per-cycle WAKE rates, which put 65 of 995 cells in another sextile); reading (b) ranks each cell's rate in each cycle's WAKE and uses the cycle that holds the analysed period.

outcomes.statement: The mean population firing rate of pE cells declines over SLEEP.
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Figure 3A and 3B
outcomes.quote: we found that the arithmetic mean of the population firing rates of pE cells declined over the course of sleep using a test of correlation of spike rate versus time ( Figure 3A-B ; R = - 0.11, p < 10 −3 )

statistics.test: correlation of spike rate versus time

outcomes.notes: Normalized mean pE rate against normalized SLEEP time, clock (i), R = -0.273 (a, p = 1.7e-13), -0.154 (b, p = 2.5e-57), -0.732 (c, p = 1.5e-09); clock (ii) R = -0.283, -0.163, -0.796. By rat (reading b) the decline is significant in 8 of 11 rats; Rizzo, Splinter and Templeton show R = -0.017, -0.049, -0.014.
deviations: Trends over normalized time follow M3 and M4 of the claims file; every reading (a, b, c) is run and, for SLEEP and episodes, two normalization clocks, (i) the period's clock time and (ii) the cumulative time of the used state, since the paper says only that SLEEP is time-normalized with nonREM time used (Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Fig. 3B legend). Values are divided by the session mean before pooling (M3).

outcomes.statement: The mean pE rate is lower in the last than in the first nonREM packet of SLEEP (1.04 against 0.88 Hz).
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep, sentence citing Vyazovskiy et al., 2009
outcomes.quote: Comparison of the population discharge rates in the first and last nonREM packets of SLEEP episodes showed an overall mean rate decrease (1.04±1.20 Hz versus 0.88±0.91 Hz; p < 0.02; Wilcoxon test)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) first 1.027 +- 1.086, last 0.905 +- 0.936 Hz, signed-rank p = 1e-18; reading (b) 1.048 and 0.883 Hz, signed-rank p = 1.9e-20, rank-sum p = 0.0012. All 51 SLEEP periods have at least 2 packets.

outcomes.statement: pE rates in the 5 min of WAKE after SLEEP are lower than in the 5 min of WAKE before.
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep
outcomes.quote: This effect was 'carried over' to subsequent WAKE as shown by the significantly decreased discharge rate of pE neurons in a 5-min post-sleep WAKE compared to a 5-min pre-sleep WAKE epoch (p < 10 −6 ; Wilcoxon test)
outcomes.notes: Only 23 cycles have a scored WAKE after their SLEEP; in 17 it starts 166 to 10344 s later. pE rates are lower after, signed-rank p = 0.018 (reading a, 703 cell-cycles) and 0.048 (b, 494 cells); rank-sum p = 0.95 and 0.98. M4 gives partial (sign right, p < 0.05, not below 1e-6). Restricted to the 6 cycles whose next WAKE starts within 1 s, signed-rank p = 0.00026. Variant, the paper's wording read as the first 5 min after SLEEP ends (47 cycles), signed-rank p = 3.9e-10 (a) and 2.8e-06 (b); on average 0.18 of those 5 min is scored as a cycle's WAKE (none in 38 cycles). Whether that is the paper's window is asked of a reader; the outcome is the claims file's reading.
deviations: The data hold scored WAKE only as the WAKE of a WAKE-SLEEP cycle, so the WAKE after a SLEEP is the next cycle's WAKE, often hours later; the variant restricted to an immediate WAKE is shown.

outcomes.statement: Comparing the same cells in the first and last nonREM packets of SLEEP, the slope of last on first rate is below 1 (95% interval 0.827 to 0.880); fast cells decrease and slow cells increase their rates over sleep.
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Figure 3D
outcomes.quote: we assessed spike rates of the same neurons in the first versus the last nonREM packets of SLEEP and found the slope of this correlation significantly departed from unity (slope 95% confidence interval 0.827-0.880)
outcomes.notes: Reading (b) slope 0.872 (0.840 to 0.904), within 0.8535 +- 0.0265; reading (a) 0.788 (0.760 to 0.817). Zero-rate cells dropped, 23 (b) and 70 (a). 72% of cells above the median first-packet rate decrease; 49% of those below increase.

outcomes.statement: Over SLEEP (nonREM only), the mean rate of the highest-rate sextiles decreases while the lowest sextile shows a marginal increase.
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Figure 3B, bottom
outcomes.quote: The mean spike discharge rate of highest-firing rate sextile groups significantly decreased over sleep whereas the activity of the lowest-firing rate sextile showed a marginal increase ( Figure 3B ; Pearson correlations versus normalized time)
deviations: Trends over normalized time follow M3 and M4 of the claims file; every reading (a, b, c) is run and, for SLEEP and episodes, two normalization clocks, (i) the period's clock time and (ii) the cumulative time of the used state, since the paper says only that SLEEP is time-normalized with nonREM time used (Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Fig. 3B legend). Values are divided by the session mean before pooling (M3).

Sextiles follow M2. Reading (a) ranks each pE cell's rate over all scored WAKE of its session (before round 1's revision, the mean of its per-cycle WAKE rates, which put 65 of 995 cells in another sextile); reading (b) ranks each cell's rate in each cycle's WAKE and uses the cycle that holds the analysed period.

outcomes.statement: The coefficient of variation of firing rates decreases over SLEEP.
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep
outcomes.quote: the coefficient of firing rate variation also showed a significantly decreasing slope over the course of SLEEP (R = - 0.05; p < 0.01)
outcomes.notes: Reading (b), the criterion's, R = -0.003, p = 0.73 (clock ii R = -0.012, p = 0.2). Variants, one point per packet R = -0.101, p = 0.0073; 50 bins clock (ii) R = -0.483, p = 0.00039; 50 bins clock (i) R = -0.025, p = 0.86.
deviations: Trends over normalized time follow M3 and M4 of the claims file; every reading (a, b, c) is run and, for SLEEP and episodes, two normalization clocks, (i) the period's clock time and (ii) the cumulative time of the used state, since the paper says only that SLEEP is time-normalized with nonREM time used (Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Fig. 3B legend). Values are divided by the session mean before pooling (M3).

outcomes.statement: Over SLEEP spindle incidence (1.94/min) decreases while spindle duration (0.52 s), frequency (13.93 Hz) and amplitude (203.3 uV) do not change.
outcomes.source: Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Figure 3C, bottom
outcomes.quote: Incidence of spindles (1.94±0.39/min) decreased (R = - 0. 093; p < 10 −5 ), while spindle duration (0.52±0.32 sec), frequency (13.93±0.93 Hz) and amplitude (203.3±87.71 µV) did not change over SLEEP

statistics.about: spindle incidence against normalized SLEEP time

outcomes.notes: Deposited spindles (5201 of 5203 start in nonREM of SLEEP); per-session mean incidence 2.852 +- 0.490 per minute, duration 0.616 s, frequency 13.923 Hz, amplitude 208.4 uV. Frequency and amplitude match; incidence matches Table S1 (0.049 Hz, 2.94 per minute) not the Results' 1.94; duration is outside 0.52 +- 0.052. Incidence over SLEEP, reading (b) R = -0.021, p = 0.03 (partial by M4); (a) p = 0.44; (c) p = 0.66; clock (ii) p >= 0.19. Absence of change holds for duration (p >= 0.068, clock i) but frequency changes under (b) (p = 0.011) and amplitude under (a) (p = 0.047). Over all 5201 spindles the duration is 0.614 +- 0.320 s, median 0.524 s, which matches the paper's 0.52 +- 0.32. With the two Dino ACC sessions left out, the incidence decrease is not significant (reading b p = 0.15).
deviations: Uses the deposited spindle detections (_Spindles.mat), reading (a) of the criterion; a new detection was not run. Amplitude converted from V to uV.

Trends over normalized time follow M3 and M4 of the claims file; every reading (a, b, c) is run and, for SLEEP and episodes, two normalization clocks, (i) the period's clock time and (ii) the cumulative time of the used state, since the paper says only that SLEEP is time-normalized with nonREM time used (Results, Firing pattern and LFP changes across the course of sleep; Fig. 3B legend). Values are divided by the session mean before pooling (M3).

The outcome depends on the normalization clock, which the paper does not state (Results; Fig. 3B legend); clock (i), the period's clock time, and clock (ii), the cumulative nonREM time, give different outcomes here. As for every trend, the outcome takes the result under one of them, as M4 does for readings; the question is put to the paper's authors.

The incidence decrease also depends on the two Dino days that were recorded with two probes and are deposited as two sessions each (ACC and mPFC); without the ACC copies, reading (b) clock (i) gives p = 0.15. Both copies are kept, since the paper's 27 sessions, which the data set matches, include them.

In addition, the fraction of time that could be identified as neither UP nor DOWN state ('other') increased significantly over the course of sleep (R = 0.08; p < 10 −2 )

findings.statement: The files hold 51 WAKE-SLEEP cycles (WakeSleepTimePairFormat over the 27 sessions), where the paper reports 54; the Wake and Sleep intervals are the same 51 pairs, with none unpaired. All other counts (995 pE, 126 pI, 27 sessions, 11 rats, 43230 UP and 86839 DOWN states, 5203 spindles) match the paper exactly.

The paper reports 790 microarousals; 434 MA intervals lie inside SLEEP (2130 MA intervals in the files, most outside SLEEP). 345 WakeInterruption intervals inside SLEEP are shorter than the 40 s minimum the data description gives for them; none lies between two packets (123 between two REM intervals, 80 between REM and a packet), so they are not MAs by the paper's definition either, though counted with the MAs they give 779 events. One nonREM packet (14 s) is shorter than the 20 s minimum of Table S1.

In Rizzo_022715 and Splinter_020515 a WAKE-SLEEP cycle's WAKE starts before the previous cycle's SLEEP ends (WAKE 9919-14394 s against SLEEP 5655-10010 s; WAKE 5335-7210 s against SLEEP 3543-5455 s), so the cycles overlap.

Dino_061914 and Dino_062014 each appear as two sessions, ACC and mPFC probes recorded at the same time (the data set's WatsonSleepHomestasis2016Table.xlsx lists the same days), each with its own state files, and the two scorings of Dino_062014 differ (mean SLEEP per cycle 59.5 min in ACC and 27.1 min in mPFC; 41 and 17 packets). State- and LFP-level analyses over the 27 sessions count these days twice.
The data description says the motion signal in _Motion.mat is z-scored; it is non-negative in every session, with per-session means from 0.55 to 4076, and BWRat19_032513 holds NaN values.

RecordingFileIntervals in _BasicMetaData.mat ends at infinity in the three sessions of rat JennBuzsaki22, and the UP/DOWN file is named _UPDOWNINtervals.mat, where the description says _UPDOWNInts.mat and _UPDOWNIntervals.mat.
The Results give spindle incidence as 1.94 +- 0.39 per minute; Table S1 gives 0.049 +- 0.008 Hz (2.94 per minute). The deposited spindles give 2.85 per minute, matching Table S1.

Scored WAKE exists only as the WAKE of a WAKE-SLEEP cycle, so the WAKE that follows a SLEEP is in most cycles absent or hours later (23 of 51 cycles have a later scored WAKE, 6 within 1 s). The 5 min post-sleep WAKE windows of the paper cannot be located for most cycles.

Each session is one tar.gz of 0.9 to 6 GB, and the order of members differs between files (the LFP .eeg comes before the spike and state files in some), so reading any one small file needs the whole archive streamed. Reading all 27 takes 7 to 9 minutes from the bucket.

Questions for the paper's authors. (1) The sampling unit of the correlations against normalized time (per packet, 10 s bins, or bins of normalized time averaged over periods) and whether SLEEP is normalized by its clock time or by its concatenated nonREM time; the readings give different outcomes for the CV, spindle and UP/DOWN trends over SLEEP. (2) Whether the burst index is the proportion of ISIs <= 15 ms (Supplemental Experimental Procedures) or the fraction of spikes with such an ISI (Results); the latter gives the reported nonREM median. (3) The model and fit range of the autocorrelogram decay exponent. (4) How triplets are formed (adjacency of scored intervals, which WAKE counts between packets, giving the 24 nonREM-WAKE-nonREM triplets) and whether REM-packet-REM triplets allow an arousal after the first REM; the attempt assumes they do, which gives 80 triplets and 660 cells against the about 136 cells of Figure S5D. (5) Whether the motion signal was z-scored before the movement correlation. (6) How the WAKE sextiles are computed for cells recorded over several cycles (session WAKE or each cycle's WAKE); fig3e-wake-before-after-sextiles and fig3f-within-up-changes differ between the two.

entries.name: watson-2016-crcns-fcx-1
entries.title: Network homeostasis and state dynamics of neocortical sleep (Watson et al. 2016)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Watson, Levenstein, Greene, Gelinas and Buzsaki (2016) on CRCNS data set fcx-1, which holds the spike trains, scored brain states, detected UP/DOWN states and spindles, and LFP of 27 frontal cortex recordings in 11 rats. It compares firing rates across states, their changes over sleep and within nonREM episodes and packets, the LFP and UP/DOWN dynamics, and the rate changes across sleep sub-state triplets.
